text: Applying for jobs is a full-time job.
Except it doesn't pay, and it's ninety percent dropdowns.
Meet Job Hunter Agent.
It does the boring part. You stay in charge of the part that matters.
Step one: answer the questions every application asks. Once.
Your name, your visa, whether you'd move to New York. Prefer not to say is always an option.
Step two: tell it your story.
Type it, say it out loud, or just drop in a résumé you secretly admire.
Say what you like about it, hit Send, and watch it rewrite your storybook in that style, line by line.
This storybook is the only thing the agent is allowed to say about you. So, no surprise PhD.
Don't love it? One click takes you back.
Every morning, it checks the job boards of the companies you care about.
Then it scores every role. Green means go, orange means maybe, and under fifty, it doesn't even bother.
Hit Prepare, and it builds a one-page résumé from your storybook.
Then it fills out the actual application. Names, dropdowns, even those tiny checkboxes nobody reads.
And when a form asks why you want to work there, it starts with their mission, not a cover-letter cliché.
And then, it stops.
Everything waits for you in the review queue.
Anything only you can answer shows up right here, with the form's own options.
Nothing goes out until you hit Approve. You're the boss. The agent is the intern who actually read the job description.
If a CAPTCHA or an email code shows up, that one's yours. It's a robot, and it's not allowed to pretend otherwise.
After you apply, it reads your inbox, read-only, and moves each application along.
Received, next step, interview, offer. Or, you know, the other one.
Under the hood, it's a simple pipeline.
Your storybook goes in. The agent finds roles, ranks them, builds the résumé, and fills the form.
You approve. It submits, tracks the replies, and learns from your notes, one small fix at a time, which you approve too.
Job Hunter Agent. Open source, and on your side.
It does the grind. You do the talking.
